newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish shares seen continuing uptrend.
newsitem.headline: Turkish shares seen continuing uptrend.

text.p: Shares trading on Istanbul's stock exchange are seen strong as prices are undervalued in dollar terms, brokers and bankers said on Monday.

"Technically, the market's first target is at $1 and the second one is at $1.3. The index's direction has turned up in dollar terms, after a medium-term downtrend (in dollar terms) for more than a year," said Resat Kutucular from Toros securities.

The IMKB-100 index closed at an all-time high of 88,079.86 on Monday, bringing the increase to 120 percent so far this year. In dollar terms, the index has gained 31.3 percent since end-1995 to $0.88, compared to a $1 record on April 8 and $0.67 at end-1995.
The lira fell below the psychologically-important 100,000 level to end at 100,500 to the dollar on Monday, against Friday's 99,645.
The Turkish currency has depreciated by 40.8 percent against the dollar since end-1995, compared to 35 percent for all of last year, showing there is room for the stock market to rally, bankers said.
They said the markets were not moved by the Turkish lira's new six-digit levels against the dollar as it was seen in line with the year-end targets for the currency.

Birol Atikol, vice president at London-based Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette investment bank, said Turkey's annual inflation running at around 80 percent made share prices very attractive for foreign investors.
"But foreign investors invest in Turkish lira when they buy shares. So they have to take into account Turkey's economic and political uncertainties," he told Reuters.

Bankers expect the lira to stand below 110,000 against the dollar at the end of 1996. Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan told a news conference on Monday that lira depreciation would stay below the inflation rate.
"Our year-end lira target is 107,000 to one dollar, unchanged from previous forecasts," said Oner Ayan from Ata securities.

Bankers said no solid developments were seen to improve the country's huge deficits which prompt heavy reliance on borrowing. Turkey's outstanding domestic debt surged to 2,891 trillion lira at end-October from 1,361 trillion lira at end-1995.
Three resource packages unveiled by the Islamist-led government since its formation in June to help plug gaping deficits have failed to inspire confidence in the markets.
The government is looking to privatisation and other revenue- raising measures to cover hefty domestic debt repayments next year, besides a significant increase in taxes.
